metadata.title: Validating automated assessments of teaching effectiveness using multimodal data

survey_design.weight_fields_interpretation: The study uses the GTI (Talis Video Study) dataset in Germany, consisting of 92 mathematics lesson videos, 46 teachers, and 1,132 students, with segment-level human ratings as training labels and student posttest mathematics achievement as an outcome. The manuscript does not report the use of complex survey weights or any student/sampling weight variables (e.g., W_FSTUWT/TOTWGT) for the ML training or the SEM predictive-validity models. Because the ML pipeline is trained on segment-level multimodal embeddings and evaluated via teacher-grouped five-fold cross-validation, the authors do not describe any weighting strategy for representativeness. For the SEM, missing data are handled via FIML, but no survey-weighted estimation is described; therefore, the analysis should be interpreted as conditional on the sampled classrooms/teachers rather than as population-representative inference.

data.handling_not_reported_explanation: The dependent variables are not PV-based cognitive achievement scores from an ILSA PV framework. Student mathematics achievement is measured using IRT weighted likelihood estimates (Warm, 1989) and the teaching-effectiveness outcomes are human/ML ratings of classroom observation subdimensions, so PV handling is not applicable. Missing data handling is addressed via Full Information Maximum Likelihood (FIML) in SEM, which is an estimation approach consistent with multiple-imputation-style handling under MAR assumptions; the paper does not provide an explicit imputation model or number of imputations, so the exact MI mechanics are not fully specified.

sample_details.sample_filtering_criteria: Analytic data come from the GTI (Talis Video Study) in Germany: 92 mathematics lesson videos focused on quadratic equations (40–90 minutes) recorded in lower secondary classrooms. Each lesson was segmented into 16-minute transcript segments (367 total segments), and two randomly assigned human raters scored each segment on 18 teaching-effectiveness subdimensions. For ML training/evaluation, segments were used with teacher-independent five-fold cross-validation where all segments from the same teacher stayed within the same fold; the ground truth for ML training was the arithmetic mean of the two human ratings. For content-validity plausibility checks, 20% of transcript segments (74) were randomly selected and evaluated by two independent expert raters using the GTI coding manual. For predictive validity, student mathematics achievement at posttest (t2) was regressed on teaching-effectiveness scores, with SEM models including teacher- and student-level covariates (Table S1 in OSF) and using FIML for missing data.

main_findings.dataset_used: GTI (Talis Video Study) Germany — lower secondary mathematics lessons on quadratic equations (segment-level; 92 lessons; 367 16-min segments)
main_findings.target_variable: Reliability of ML-generated teaching effectiveness subdimension scores (absolute accuracy, relative accuracy, bias)
main_findings.performance_metrics: Reliability (Table 2): ML text+audio models showed higher absolute accuracy than human ratings for 11/18 subdimensions; bias was lower for humans in 12/18 subdimensions. Examples: Monitoring (human AA=0.690 vs ML text AA=0.377; ML text+audio AA=0.335; ML text+audio+video AA=0.381). Classroom management bias positive for ML across routines, monitoring, disruptions (humans higher).
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using GTI (Talis Video Study) Germany segment-level multimodal the study leveraged teacher and student background covariates alongside modality-specific ML scoring pipelines to predict reliability of teaching-effectiveness subdimension scores, finding that text- and text+audio-based ML models were often more reliable than human ratings on absolute accuracy for 11/18 subdimensions while humans showed less bias in 12/18 subdimensions. This indicates that multimodal ML can improve scoring consistency for many instructional subdimensions, but human-like systematic bias patterns still need calibration before operational use.

main_findings.dataset_used: GTI (Talis Video Study) Germany — lower secondary mathematics lessons on quadratic equations (74 transcript segments for plausibility evaluation)
main_findings.target_variable: Content validity of ML-generated teaching effectiveness subdimension scores (expert plausibility; Cohen’s kappa)
main_findings.performance_metrics: Content validity (Table 3): mean Cohen’s kappa across 18 subdimensions kmean = 0.125 (just acceptable for clarity and understanding of procedures/processes). Across all subdimensions, ML scores were rated more plausible on average (Rater 1: 54.16%, Rater 2: 53.85%). Highest plausibility for engagement in cognitively demanding subject matter (Rater 1: 63.64%, Rater 2: 78.18%).
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using GTI Germany transcript-segment the study leveraged teacher and student background covariates together with modality-specific ML-generated scores to predict expert plausibility judgments, finding that experts slightly favored ML-generated scores overall (about 54% of decisions) despite very low agreement between the two expert raters (kappa mean = 0.125). This indicates that ML-generated teaching-effectiveness scores can be content-valid in the sense of aligning with human intuition, but content-validity evaluation reliability remains a major bottleneck for scaling.

main_findings.dataset_used: GTI (Talis Video Study) Germany — lower secondary mathematics lessons on quadratic equations (student posttest t2; SEM predictive validity)
main_findings.target_variable: Predictive validity of ML-generated teaching effectiveness subdimension scores for student mathematics achievement (posttest)
main_findings.performance_metrics: SEM results (Table 4; adjusted standardized slopes b*adj): Human-generated scores significant positive for Questioning (b*adj=0.22, p<.001) and Understanding procedures/processes (b*adj=0.40, p<.001); significant negative for Explicit patterns/generalizations (b*adj=-0.24, p=0.004) and Student-aligned instruction (b*adj=-0.28, p<.001). ML text model significant positive for Disruptions (b*adj=0.30, p=0.025), Clarity (b*adj=0.15, p<.001), Eliciting student thinking (b*adj=0.28, p=0.013); significant negative for Monitoring (b*adj=-0.42, p<.001), Encouragement/warmth (b*adj=-0.40, p=0.003), Multiple approaches/reasoning (b*adj=-0.24, p<.001). ML text+audio model significant positive for Routines (b*adj=0.33, p=0.003) and Engagement in cognitively demanding subject matter (b*adj=0.30, p<.001); significant negative for Encouragement/warmth (b*adj=-0.13, p=0.009) and Multiple approaches/reasoning (b*adj=-0.47, p<.001). Model with all three modalities (text+audio+video) had no statistically significant relationships after Benjamini–Hochberg correction.
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using GTI Germany student posttest achievement the study leveraged teacher and student background covariates and modality-specific ML-generated teaching-effectiveness subdimensions to predict mathematics achievement, finding that predictive validity was inconsistent across subdimensions and modalities and that the all-three-modality model showed no significant associations after false-discovery-rate control. This indicates that ML-based teaching scores may be useful for reliability and plausibility, but their direct predictive utility for student achievement requires subdimension- and modality-specific refinement rather than assuming that adding modalities automatically improves validity.

data.outcome_summary: This study uses the GTI (Talis Video Study) dataset in Germany, focusing on lower-secondary mathematics lessons on quadratic equations. It trains multimodal neural models on 367 16-minute lesson segments to generate scores for 18 teaching-effectiveness subdimensions, using the arithmetic mean of two human raters as ground truth, and evaluates generalizability with teacher-grouped five-fold cross-validation. For reliability (RQ1), ML scores based on text and text+audio often matched or exceeded human ratings in absolute accuracy for 11/18 subdimensions, while humans showed lower bias in 12/18 subdimensions. For content validity (RQ2), expert plausibility judgments slightly favored ML overall (~54%), but expert agreement was very low (mean kappa = 0.125). For predictive validity (RQ3), adjusted SEM slopes showed mixed positive and negative associations for specific subdimensions, and the text+audio+video model had no significant relationships after Benjamini–Hochberg correction. Limitations include reliance on human ratings as labels and the absence of survey-weighted, population-representative inference.
